newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Former Central African emperor Bokassa dead.
newsitem.headline: Former Central African emperor Bokassa dead.

text.p: Jean-Bedel Bokassa, former self-syled emperor of the Central African Republic, has died at the age of 75, closing a colourful and sometimes grim chapter in the diamond-rich yet impoverished nation's history.

One of Bokassa's sons, Jean Charles, announced the news early on Monday. The flamboyant former leader, who had been ill with kidney, suspected cerebral and other problems, died of a heart attack on Sunday night in the capital Bangui.

"Bokassa played a very important role for his country," opposition Patriotic Front for Progress leader Abel Goumba told Reuters, adding that his "monarchic and dictatorial regime" had also caused a lot of harm.
Bokassa, whose rule was one of cruelty and extravagance punctuated by capricious decisions, seized power in 1966.

Modelling himself on his hero Napoleon Bonaparte of France, he crowned himself emperor in a ceremony in 1977. His crown alone was worth $5 million and the ceremony reputedly swallowed a quarter of the country's annual foreign exchange earnings.
Ousted in a French-backed coup in 1979 while in Libya, he lived in exile in Ivory Coast and former colonial power France.
In 1986 he suddenly returned to the Central African Republic, where he was sentenced to death in 1987 for murder and embezzlement after a trial coloured by accusations of infanticide and cannibalism.
The military leader at the time, Andre Kolingba, commuted Bokassa's sentence to life in prison and then freed him in 1993 at the height of a transition to multi-party democracy.
Bokassa remained convinced of his popularity with the masses until the end, harbouring hopes of being allowed to stage a comeback via presidential elections scheduled for 1999.
"Whenever I go out, a large gathering collects about me out of adoration, so I seldom go out," he told Reuters in an interview at his home in the capital Bangui in May.
Around that time he wrote to President Ange-Felix Patasse asking for a formal amnesty so that he could run for president.

"His majesty Bokassa the First hopes that his request will be favourably received to enable him to stand as a candidate in the next presidential elections according to the principle of democracy, in line with the wishes of the majority of the Central African people," he said in the letter.
Bokassa, a fervent Roman Catholic who fathered at least 55 children, once flirted with the idea of becoming a priest.
Instead he became a soldier in France's colonial army. He was armed forces chief of staff when he toppled his nephew David Dacko, the nation's independence president.
Bokassa had been receiving medical care at home since returning to the Central African Republic in mid-October after about two weeks of intensive care in a private clinic in Ivory Coast.
Medical sources in Ivory Coast suggested he might need surgery to remove a brain tumour, but his son said on his return to Bangui that he had simply been been put on kidney dialysis in Abidjan.

Bokassa, who lived quietly in Bangui on his French army pension following his release from jail, but during an army pay revolt in May he joined critics of France, which stepped in under a defence pact to keep Patasse in power.
"Why does France intervene in our country at every little problem, why ? Perhaps because of the diamonds," he said.
